To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary protein and celluloses concentrations affect the composition and concentration of volatile fatty acids, phenol, indole, N2O, and DM in swine manure.
reducing dietary CP or increasing dietary cellulose concentration in swine diets can affect the composition of manure, which may affect the impact of livestock production systems on the environment.
reducing dietary CP or increasing dietary cellulose concentration can alter the chemical characteristics of swine manure, which can affect its potential to affect soil, air, or water quality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
reducing the environmental impact of swine manure by reducing N, S, C, and VFA excretion, while maintaining the nutritional quality of swine manures.
the effect of diet composition (CP and cellulose) on manure composition and the environmental impact of swine manure on soil, air and water.
the effect of dietary CP and/or fiber on manure composition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
decreasing dietary CP or increasing dietary cellulose can affect manure composition, and these effects may have environmental consequences.
reducing the dietary CP and increasing the dietary cellulose content of the diet of growing pigs results in manure of lower N concentration and higher C:N ratio.
decreasing dietary CP concentration increased manure pH, NH4, phenol, isovaleric acid, and cresol concentrations, but decreasing dietary CP concentration reduced acetic acid concentration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the manure from pigs fed a diet containing 12% CP had a greater concentration of N and a greater potential to emit N2O, but a lower concentration of NH4 and a greater potential for N retention in the manure compared with the manure of pigs fed a diet with 14.5% CP.

the effects of reducing CP and increasing cellulose in the diets of growing swine are to increase the concentration of C, N2O, and VFA, and to decrease the concentrations of NH4, isovaleric acid, phenol, 4-ethylphenol, and pH in manure.
the addition of cellulose to the diet can reduce manure N and increase manure C, but that this effect is offset by increased manure DM and N excretion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the manure from pigs fed low-protein diets and low levels of dietary cellulose has a higher pH and lower concentrations of N, NH4, and indoles, which may be more desirable for land application of swine manure.
reducing dietary CP and/or increasing dietary cellulose can reduce the environmental impact of swine production by reducing N and C losses from the manure.
reducing the protein content of the diet will reduce the concentration of phenol and indole in the manure, which may reduce the impact of manure on water quality.
